summary: Provides terminology for benchmarking LAN switching devices. It extends the terminology of RFC 1242 and RFC 1944 to switches. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a dictionary of shared words so everyone talks about testing network switches the same way.

questions: how to benchmark a network switch
how do you measure switch performance
subtitle: A shared vocabulary for measuring and comparing the performance of network switches.

tldr.problem: Network switches are tested and evaluated by many vendors and operators, but without standard terminology, benchmark results are hard to compare and understand across different reports.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines precise terms for test traffic patterns (unidirectional, bidirectional, meshed), load conditions (intended load, offered load, maximum load), forwarding performance metrics, and behaviors like congestion control, address learning, and broadcast handling.
tldr.outcome: Engineers and operators can now read switch benchmarks and understand exactly what was tested and how—enabling fair comparison between switches and informed purchasing decisions.

today: RFC 2285 remains the authoritative terminology reference for LAN switch benchmarking. The switch market has evolved toward higher speeds and modular architectures, but the fundamental concepts and metrics defined here are still used in benchmarking reports and vendor datasheets. It is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Testing Language for Switches
sections.content:
Network switches forward frames at the MAC (Media Access Control) layer. When evaluating switches, vendors and operators need to measure their performance under various conditions: how many frames per second can a switch forward? How much does congestion on one port affect traffic on another? How quickly can a switch learn new addresses?

Without shared terminology, these benchmarks become confusing. One vendor's measurement of "throughput" might not match another's; terms like "congestion control" mean different things to different testers. RFC 2285 solves this by defining a comprehensive glossary specifically for LAN switch benchmarking, extending earlier work on general network device benchmarking (RFC 1242 and RFC 1944) to the specifics of switching.
sections.plainLanguage: A switch is like a postal worker who looks at mail addresses and routes each letter to the right door. You need to know: how fast does the worker deliver mail? What happens when everyone sends mail at once? Does some mail get lost? To answer fairly, you need the same definition of these words every time.

sections.title: How Test Traffic Moves
sections.content:
The RFC defines how traffic flows through a switch during testing in two dimensions: orientation and distribution.

Orientation describes whether traffic flows in one direction or both. Unidirectional traffic enters on some input interfaces and exits on different, non-overlapping output interfaces—useful for measuring throughput and detecting congestion effects. Bidirectional traffic flows both directions on the same interfaces, mimicking full-duplex real-world use.

Distribution describes how traffic maps between inputs and outputs. Non-meshed traffic is one-to-one: input A talks only to output A. Partially meshed allows many-to-one, one-to-many, or many-to-many patterns. Fully meshed means every input interface sends frames to every other interface, stressing the entire switch simultaneously.

The RFC also defines bursts of frames separated by gaps, and loads: the intended load (what the tester tries to send) and the offered load (what actually gets sent, accounting for collisions or flow control). These distinctions matter because on half-duplex media, the tester may not achieve its intended load.
sections.plainLanguage: In a one-way test, packages come in one door and leave another. In a two-way test, they go back and forth. A busy test sends to everyone at once. And sometimes you aim for 100 packages but only 80 actually make it—the switch's fault or the test device's?

sections.title: Measuring Switch Performance
sections.content:
The RFC defines three key forwarding rate metrics. Forwarding rate (FR) is simply the number of frames per second a switch successfully transmits to the correct destination in response to a given offered load. Maximum forwarding rate (MFR) is the highest forwarding rate achieved across all test loads. Forwarding rate at maximum offered load (FRMOL) is the forwarding rate specifically when traffic hits the maximum load the test device can push.

These three metrics reveal different aspects of switch behavior. A switch might handle moderate loads well but degrade under peak load, in which case MFR and FRMOL will differ. This distinction is important for network planning.

The RFC also covers address handling: how many MAC addresses can a switch cache? How fast can it learn new ones? Broadcast handling measures how a switch forwards broadcasts to all interfaces in a domain, and the latency of broadcast delivery. Error filtering examines whether the switch properly discards oversized frames, undersized frames, and frames with corrupted checksums. Finally, congestion control looks at techniques like backpressure (slowing the tester) and forward pressure (aggressive medium access), and phenomena like head-of-line blocking (congestion on one input affecting other inputs).
sections.plainLanguage: Three key numbers: how many packets per second at normal load, at peak load, and at maximum pressure. Also, does the switch learn addresses fast? Does it handle broken packets? When one port is jammed, does it slow down the others?

sections.title: How to Report Results Fairly
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that benchmark results must be reported with context. For instance, forwarding rate must always be reported alongside the offered load that produced it—otherwise the number is meaningless. Similarly, maximum offered load must be cited when reporting forwarding rate at maximum load.

The RFC notes that some switch behaviors complicate testing. For example, a switch using backpressure (IEEE 802.3x flow control on full-duplex Ethernet) may exhibit zero frame loss when the tester tries to overload it. However, this does not mean the switch can exceed the media's maximum rate; backpressure simply tells the tester to slow down. Testers must account for the difference between intended load (what they try to send) and offered load (what actually gets sent), especially when half-duplex collisions or flow control are in play.

The RFC also covers edge cases: bridges may generate spanning tree BPDUs (Bridge Protocol Data Units) or SNMP frames that appear on interfaces but were not part of the test. These must be handled carefully when computing forwarding statistics.
sections.plainLanguage: When you report a number, explain the test conditions too. If a switch doesn't drop packets but slows you down to avoid overload, that's not the same as the switch being super fast—you have to say what the test device really managed to send.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content:
Switch benchmarking is not just an academic exercise. Network operators evaluating switches for deployment want to know how much traffic a switch can handle, how it behaves when overloaded, how quickly it learns MAC addresses (important when the network restarts), and whether it correctly filters malformed frames that might indicate attacks or faults.

Vendors also use this terminology to publish fair, reproducible benchmarks that buyers can trust. By adhering to the same definitions, vendors signal that their tests are conducted with integrity and that buyers can compare results across products.

The RFC acknowledges that different vendors may adopt different strategies—some optimize for forwarding rate at any cost, others prioritize latency stability or broadcast performance—but the terminology allows all these different optimization goals to be measured and compared on the same standard terms.
sections.plainLanguage: Knowing these terms helps you choose the right switch for your network. And vendors who publish clear benchmarks using the right words are more trustworthy—you know what you're getting.
